blocks.content: The story starts with a mess that every growing engineering team eventually creates.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276412866-477728924.png
blocks.alt: Clients calling multiple backend services directly without a gateway

blocks.content: You started with one backend service. Then you added authentication. Then a payments service. Then notifications. Then a search service. Each one speaks slightly differently different auth mechanisms, different rate limits, different response formats.

Your mobile app talks to six different services directly. Your web frontend talks to eight. Every client has to know where every service lives, how to authenticate with each one, and how to handle each one's error format.
Then a new intern joins and asks: "Why does the mobile app call auth.internal:3001/validate directly?"
Nobody has a good answer.

This is the problem API Gateways solve. Instead of every client knowing about every service, you put one front door on your entire backend. Everything goes through it. The gateway handles the common concerns authentication, rate limiting, routing, logging so your backend services don't have to.
1. What an API Gateway actually is
blocks.text: 1. What an API Gateway actually is

blocks.content: An API Gateway is a reverse proxy with a brain. A basic reverse proxy forwards requests to backends. An API Gateway inspects, transforms, authenticates, rate-limits, and routes requests before a single line of your application code runs.
It sits between every client and every backend service. Clients talk to one address. The gateway figures out everything else.
Without Gateway
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276415451-253533017.png
blocks.alt: Three clients each calling three backend services directly

blocks.content: Imagine you have three clients: a mobile app, a web application, and a third-party application. You also have three backend services: Auth Service, Order Service, and User Service.

Without an API Gateway, every client has to communicate directly with every service. The mobile app must know where the Auth Service is running, where the Order Service is running, and where the User Service is running. The web application must know the same information, and so does the third-party application.

As the system grows, this becomes messy. If the address of a service changes, every client must be updated. Authentication, security checks, and request validation often get repeated across multiple services. Over time, managing all these direct connections becomes difficult and error-prone.
This is why the left side is called chaos too many connections and too much responsibility spread across different clients.
With Gateway
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276417398-552649464.png
blocks.alt: Clients calling a single API gateway which routes to backend services

blocks.content: Now introduce an API Gateway in front of all services.
Instead of talking directly to Auth Service, Order Service, and User Service, every client talks only to the API Gateway. The gateway becomes the single entry point for the entire system.

When a request arrives, the gateway checks authentication, applies rate limits, performs logging, and then forwards the request to the correct backend service. If the client wants user information, the gateway sends the request to User Service. If it needs order information, the gateway sends it to Order Service.
From the client's perspective, there is only one address to remember: the API Gateway.

This creates order because all common responsibilities are handled in one place, backend services remain hidden from the outside world, and clients no longer need to know where individual services are running.
2. What an API Gateway does
Every request that arrives at the gateway passes through a pipeline of concerns. These execute in order, and any step can reject the request before it ever reaches your backend.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520240-153894742.png
blocks.alt: API gateway performing auth rate limit and routing checks before reaching backend

blocks.content: When a client sends a request, it doesn't directly reach the backend service. Instead, it first passes through the API Gateway. The gateway acts like a security guard, traffic controller, validator, and router all in one place. Every request goes through a series of steps before it is allowed to enter the system.

blocks.content: 1. TLS Termination

The request arrives over HTTPS. The API Gateway decrypts the encrypted traffic and handles SSL certificates on behalf of all backend services. This means individual services don't need to manage certificates themselves.
2. Authentication
Next, the gateway verifies the identity of the caller. It checks JWT tokens, API keys, session tokens, or OAuth credentials.
If authentication fails, the gateway immediately returns a 401 Unauthorized response and stops processing. The request never reaches the backend.
3. Rate Limiting
Once the user is authenticated, the gateway checks whether the client is sending too many requests.
For example, if a client is allowed only 100 requests per minute and sends 500 requests, the gateway blocks the excess traffic and returns 429 Too Many Requests.
This protects backend services from abuse, bots, and sudden traffic spikes.
4. Request Validation
The gateway then validates the request itself.
It checks whether required headers are present, whether parameters are valid, and whether the request body follows the expected format.
If the request is invalid, the gateway returns 400 Bad Request immediately instead of wasting backend resources.
5. Routing Decision
Now the request is trusted and valid. The gateway decides which backend service should handle it. A request for:
/api/auth/login
goes to the Auth Service. A request for:
/api/orders
goes to the Order Service. A request for:
/api/users
goes to the User Service. The client never needs to know where these services are actually running.
6. Transformation
Before forwarding the request, the gateway can modify it if necessary.
It may add headers, convert formats, inject user information from the token, or transform the request into a format expected by the backend service.
This keeps backend services simpler because they receive a consistent request format.
Backend Service
Only after passing all previous checks does the request finally reach the backend service.
The service receives a clean, authenticated, validated request and can focus entirely on business logic instead of worrying about security, rate limiting, or request validation.
7. Response Handling
After the backend generates a response, the gateway processes it before sending it back to the client.
It can compress data, cache responses, transform formats, or add response headers.
8. Logging and Tracing
Throughout the entire journey, the gateway records important information such as request time, response time, status codes, user IDs, and latency.
This makes monitoring, debugging, and troubleshooting much easier.
In Short
The API Gateway acts as a single front door for the entire system.
Instead of every microservice implementing authentication, rate limiting, validation, logging, and routing separately, the gateway handles these concerns once in a centralized place.
As a result, backend services remain simple and focused on business logic, while the gateway takes care of everything related to traffic management, security, and communication.
3. The six core capabilities
1. Authentication and authorisation
The gateway is the only public entry point. Every request must prove who it is before reaching a backend. The gateway validates tokens centrally so individual services don't have to.

["JWT validation: the gateway decodes the token, verifies the signature against the public key, checks expiry. If valid, it extracts claims (user ID, roles, scopes) and forwards them as headers to the backend (X-User-Id: 12345, X-User-Role: admin). The backend trusts these headers it never sees the raw token.
","API key authentication: for machine-to-machine calls. The gateway checks the key against a database, maps it to a client identity and permissions. The backend receives a cleaned-up identity, not the raw key.
","OAuth2 / OIDC: for third-party integrations. The gateway acts as the OAuth resource server, validating access tokens from external identity providers.
"]
items: JWT validation: the gateway decodes the token, verifies the signature against the public key, checks expiry. If valid, it extracts claims (user ID, roles, scopes) and forwards them as headers to the backend (X-User-Id: 12345, X-User-Role: admin). The backend trusts these headers it never sees the raw token.

API key authentication: for machine-to-machine calls. The gateway checks the key against a database, maps it to a client identity and permissions. The backend receives a cleaned-up identity, not the raw key.
OAuth2 / OIDC: for third-party integrations. The gateway acts as the OAuth resource server, validating access tokens from external identity providers.

blocks.content: 2. Rate limiting
The gateway enforces how many requests a client can make in a time window. Without this, one abusive client can take down your entire backend.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276423649-823404760.png
blocks.alt: Gateway checking request quota and allowing or rejecting with 429

blocks.content:
["Per-user rate limiting: each authenticated user gets a quota. X-User-Id: 12345 is allowed 1,000 requests per minute.
","Per-API-key limiting: for developer APIs. Free tier gets 100 req/min. Pro tier gets 10,000 req/min. Enterprise gets unlimited. The gateway checks the key's tier and applies the corresponding limit.
","Per-endpoint limiting: expensive endpoints (search, export, report generation) get stricter limits than cheap ones (read a profile).
","Global rate limiting: a circuit breaker that protects the entire system if overall traffic spikes beyond what backends can handle.
"]
items: Per-user rate limiting: each authenticated user gets a quota. X-User-Id: 12345 is allowed 1,000 requests per minute.
Per-API-key limiting: for developer APIs. Free tier gets 100 req/min. Pro tier gets 10,000 req/min. Enterprise gets unlimited. The gateway checks the key's tier and applies the corresponding limit.
Per-endpoint limiting: expensive endpoints (search, export, report generation) get stricter limits than cheap ones (read a profile).
Global rate limiting: a circuit breaker that protects the entire system if overall traffic spikes beyond what backends can handle.

blocks.content: 3. Routing
The gateway inspects the request and decides which backend service handles it. This is what makes one URL space across many services possible.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276425430-297019992.png
blocks.alt: Gateway inspecting request path and routing to the matching backend service

blocks.content: Routing can also be on: HTTP method, query params, request headers,client IP, custom claims from JWT, A/B test assignment, weighted traffic split
Weighted routing deserves special mention. When you deploy a new version, you don't flip all traffic at once.
You give V2 a 5% weight and V1 a 95% weight. The gateway randomly assigns requests in that ratio. You watch metrics.
If V2 is healthy, you shift to 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%. If V2 breaks, you flip back to 0% instantly one config change, no deployment needed.
This is canary deployment, and the gateway is what makes it possible without touching your services.
4. Request and response transformation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276427152-58090396.png
blocks.alt: Gateway transforming request and response formats between client and backend

blocks.content: Clients often need data in a different format than what backends naturally produce. The gateway can translate between them without either side changing.

["Protocol translation: client sends REST/HTTP, backend speaks gRPC. The gateway translates between them. Or client sends JSON, legacy backend expects XML gateway converts.
","Header manipulation: strip internal headers before sending to client, inject tracing headers before sending to backend, add CORS headers to every response.
","Request enrichment: client sends a user ID, gateway fetches the user's profile and attaches it to the request before it reaches the backend. The backend service doesn't need to do that lookup.
","Response filtering: backend returns a large object with 50 fields. The mobile client only needs 8 of them. The gateway strips the rest. Reduces payload size, reduces parsing work on the client.
"]
items: Protocol translation: client sends REST/HTTP, backend speaks gRPC. The gateway translates between them. Or client sends JSON, legacy backend expects XML gateway converts.
Header manipulation: strip internal headers before sending to client, inject tracing headers before sending to backend, add CORS headers to every response.
Request enrichment: client sends a user ID, gateway fetches the user's profile and attaches it to the request before it reaches the backend. The backend service doesn't need to do that lookup.
Response filtering: backend returns a large object with 50 fields. The mobile client only needs 8 of them. The gateway strips the rest. Reduces payload size, reduces parsing work on the client.

blocks.content: 5. Observability: logging, metrics, tracing
Every request passes through the gateway. This makes it the perfect place to emit observability data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276428980-642534721.png
blocks.alt: Gateway emitting logs metrics and traces for every request

blocks.content: Every request automatically gets:

["A trace ID assigned and propagated to the backend via X-Trace-Id header","Request logged: timestamp, client ID, endpoint, status code, latency","Metrics emitted: request count, error rate, p50/p99 latency per endpoint per client"]
items: A trace ID assigned and propagated to the backend via X-Trace-Id header
Request logged: timestamp, client ID, endpoint, status code, latency
Metrics emitted: request count, error rate, p50/p99 latency per endpoint per client

blocks.content: Your dashboards show you before touching a single backend exactly which endpoints are slow, which clients are hammering you, where errors are spiking. One instrumentation point covers your entire API surface.

blocks.content: 6. Circuit breaking and resilience
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276430734-612493421.png
blocks.alt: Circuit breaker moving between closed open and test states

blocks.content: Normally, the API Gateway forwards requests to the backend service.

If the backend starts returning too many errors or becomes very slow, the gateway opens the circuit and immediately stops sending requests to that service. Instead, clients receive a quick 503 Service Unavailable response.
After a short wait, the gateway sends a few test requests (Half-Open state) to check whether the backend has recovered.
["If the tests fail, the circuit stays open.","If the tests succeed, the circuit closes and normal traffic resumes."]
items: If the tests fail, the circuit stays open.
If the tests succeed, the circuit closes and normal traffic resumes.

blocks.content: In simple terms: A circuit breaker temporarily blocks traffic to a failing service, gives it time to recover, and automatically restores traffic when the service becomes healthy again.
Request lifecycle: end to end
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520241-694298266.png
blocks.alt: End to end request lifecycle through authentication rate limiting routing and transform

blocks.content: The gateway overhead is typically 1–5ms. For any non-trivial backend operation (database queries, business logic), this is invisible. The benefits centralised auth, rate limiting, observability are worth orders of magnitude more than 2ms.
4. API versioning through the gateway
One of the most practical uses of the gateway is managing API versions without disrupting clients.

/api/v1/users/{id}  →  user-service-v1:3001
/api/v2/users/{id}  →  user-service-v2:3002
/api/users/{id}     →  user-service-v2:3002  (latest)
V1 and V2 run simultaneously. Old clients keep working unchanged. New clients use V2.
When you're confident V1 is unused (metrics tell you), you deprecate it first return aDeprecationheader, then return 410 Gone, then remove the route.
The gateway is the enforcer of this lifecycle. Backend code doesn't need to handle multiple versions in the same codebase.
5. API Gateway vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer
blocks.text: 5. API Gateway vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer

blocks.content: These are often confused. They serve different purposes at different layers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520241-256999116.png
blocks.alt: Load balancer gateway and reverse proxy layered in front of backend services

blocks.content: In practice: you often have all three. A load balancer distributes traffic across gateway instances. The gateway handles auth/routing/rate-limiting. A reverse proxy (nginx) might sit alongside for static asset serving or TLS.
6. Where API Gateways are tricky

["The gateway becomes a single point of failure. If one pod handles all traffic and crashes, everything is down. You must run multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer. Horizontally scale it. The shared state (rate limiting counters, circuit breaker state) lives in Redis, not in the gateway process itself.
","Latency budget. Every step in the pipeline adds latency. JWT validation, Redis lookup for rate limiting, routing table evaluation. For high-frequency trading or real-time gaming, 2ms of gateway overhead is unacceptable. In those cases you often need a lighter gateway or bypass it for internal service calls.
","The gateway knows too much. If the gateway handles authentication, authorisation, rate limiting, routing, transformation, circuit breaking, observability it becomes a fat middleware that's hard to reason about and slow to deploy changes to. Teams often split this across a lightweight gateway (routing + auth) and a service mesh (service-to-service concerns).
","Internal service calls bypass the gateway. Service A calling Service B internally should not go through the public gateway that adds unnecessary latency and the traffic is already inside your trusted network. This is where a service mesh (Istio, Envoy) handles service-to-service communication while the API Gateway handles external client traffic."]
items: The gateway becomes a single point of failure. If one pod handles all traffic and crashes, everything is down. You must run multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer. Horizontally scale it. The shared state (rate limiting counters, circuit breaker state) lives in Redis, not in the gateway process itself.

Latency budget. Every step in the pipeline adds latency. JWT validation, Redis lookup for rate limiting, routing table evaluation. For high-frequency trading or real-time gaming, 2ms of gateway overhead is unacceptable. In those cases you often need a lighter gateway or bypass it for internal service calls.

The gateway knows too much. If the gateway handles authentication, authorisation, rate limiting, routing, transformation, circuit breaking, observability it becomes a fat middleware that's hard to reason about and slow to deploy changes to. Teams often split this across a lightweight gateway (routing + auth) and a service mesh (service-to-service concerns).

Internal service calls bypass the gateway. Service A calling Service B internally should not go through the public gateway that adds unnecessary latency and the traffic is already inside your trusted network. This is where a service mesh (Istio, Envoy) handles service-to-service communication while the API Gateway handles external client traffic.

blocks.content: 7. Real-world tools

["AWS API Gateway: managed, serverless-friendly, tight AWS integration. Great for Lambda backends. Per-request pricing can be expensive at high scale.
","Kong: open source, highly extensible plugin ecosystem. Runs on nginx. Can run self-hosted or managed. Most popular for teams that want control.
","Apigee (Google): enterprise-grade, strong analytics and developer portal. Common in large enterprises with complex API products.
","nginx + custom middleware: teams that want maximum control write their own gateway logic on top of nginx. More work, total flexibility.
","Envoy: not a gateway itself, but the proxy engine behind many gateways (Istio, AWS App Mesh). Configuration-heavy but extremely powerful.
","Traefik / Caddy: lightweight, good for Kubernetes environments. Simpler feature set, easier to operate.
"]
items: AWS API Gateway: managed, serverless-friendly, tight AWS integration. Great for Lambda backends. Per-request pricing can be expensive at high scale.
Kong: open source, highly extensible plugin ecosystem. Runs on nginx. Can run self-hosted or managed. Most popular for teams that want control.
Apigee (Google): enterprise-grade, strong analytics and developer portal. Common in large enterprises with complex API products.
nginx + custom middleware: teams that want maximum control write their own gateway logic on top of nginx. More work, total flexibility.
Envoy: not a gateway itself, but the proxy engine behind many gateways (Istio, AWS App Mesh). Configuration-heavy but extremely powerful.
Traefik / Caddy: lightweight, good for Kubernetes environments. Simpler feature set, easier to operate.

blocks.content: 8. HLD interview: how to talk about this
blocks.text: 8. HLD interview: how to talk about this

blocks.content: When designing any system with multiple services and external clients, bring the API Gateway in early:

["State the problem it solves. \"We have multiple backend services and several types of clients mobile, web, third-party developers. Without a gateway, every client needs to know about every service, and auth/rate-limiting logic is duplicated everywhere. I'd put an API Gateway as the single entry point.\"
","Name the specific capabilities your system needs. Don't list everything  pick what's relevant. For a ride-sharing app: \"The gateway handles JWT auth, rate limits the search endpoint heavily since it's expensive, routes /driver calls to the driver service and /rider calls to the rider service, and emits traces for every request.\"
","Address the single point of failure. \"The gateway itself runs as multiple instances behind a load balancer. Rate limiting state lives in Redis so it's consistent across all gateway pods. If one gateway pod goes down, the load balancer routes to the others no service disruption.\"
","Distinguish it from a service mesh. \"The API Gateway handles north-south traffic external clients into the system. Service-to-service calls inside the cluster bypass the gateway and go through a service mesh Envoy sidecars handling mTLS, retry logic, and distributed tracing between services.\"
","Mention what stays out of the gateway. \"Business logic stays out of the gateway. The gateway knows nothing about orders or users it just authenticates, rate limits, and routes. That keeps the gateway thin and fast.\"
"]
items: State the problem it solves. "We have multiple backend services and several types of clients mobile, web, third-party developers. Without a gateway, every client needs to know about every service, and auth/rate-limiting logic is duplicated everywhere. I'd put an API Gateway as the single entry point."

Name the specific capabilities your system needs. Don't list everything  pick what's relevant. For a ride-sharing app: "The gateway handles JWT auth, rate limits the search endpoint heavily since it's expensive, routes /driver calls to the driver service and /rider calls to the rider service, and emits traces for every request."

Address the single point of failure. "The gateway itself runs as multiple instances behind a load balancer. Rate limiting state lives in Redis so it's consistent across all gateway pods. If one gateway pod goes down, the load balancer routes to the others no service disruption."

Distinguish it from a service mesh. "The API Gateway handles north-south traffic external clients into the system. Service-to-service calls inside the cluster bypass the gateway and go through a service mesh Envoy sidecars handling mTLS, retry logic, and distributed tracing between services."

Mention what stays out of the gateway. "Business logic stays out of the gateway. The gateway knows nothing about orders or users it just authenticates, rate limits, and routes. That keeps the gateway thin and fast."

blocks.content: The strongest interview answers treat the gateway as one component in a layered architecture not a magic box that solves everything, but a precisely scoped component that handles cross-cutting concerns at the edge so your services don't have to.
